strengths: The method addresses a valuable computer vision problem: constructing compact training datasets at ImageNet scale without expensive bilevel differentiation. Combining representative feature targets with per-class BatchNorm regularization is a practical design.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements across several settings: 38.2% ImageNet-1K accuracy at 10 images per class versus 32.1% for SCDD, and 59.4% on Tiny ImageNet at 50 images per class versus 48.7% for CDA. Repeated runs and cross-architecture experiments strengthen the empirical evidence.

The factorial ablation supports complementary benefits from feature matching and per-class BatchNorm. With PCBN fixed, replacing cross-entropy with the proposed feature loss improves all three datasets. Layer, regularization-strength, and sliced-Wasserstein experiments provide additional useful analysis.

The pipeline is clearly organized, with pseudocode, implementation settings, informative visualizations, and a code link. Core datasets and inherited methods are credited, and the societal-impact discussion appropriately acknowledges inherited dataset biases.
weaknesses: The central contribution needs clearer positioning against classical quantization. For the implemented squared-Euclidean objective, one input distribution and freely optimized support weights make Eqs. (5)–(6) equivalent to k-means quantization: minimizing the average squared distance to the nearest prototype. A k-means-prototype inversion baseline with identical PCBN and training, together with a learned-versus-uniform-weight ablation, is needed to establish the benefit of the proposed solver.

The MMD comparison does not isolate the metric. At one image per class, the squared-Wasserstein target is exactly the class feature mean, making Eq. (12) identical to linear-kernel mean matching when the encoder is held fixed. Consequently, Figure 4's 5.77% versus 0.48% gap cannot establish a geometric advantage of Wasserstein alone. Section 5.6 acknowledges different encoder regimes; removing augmentations and FKD does not control this difference.

The baseline protocols require reconciliation. At ImageNet-1K 10 IPC, Table 4's CE+BN control achieves 35.9%, whereas Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L despite describing comparisons as using identical settings. The manuscript does not explain this substantial discrepancy. Matched teacher, relabeling, and student-training protocols are necessary to establish how much of the headline improvement comes from the proposed components.

The stated solver contains a consequential inconsistency. Algorithm 2 updates the weights after computing the transport plan, then reuses that plan for the position update, although Eq. (11) assumes its column sums equal the current weights. Simplex projection can also produce zero weights, making the inverse Hessian undefined. Transport recomputation, zero-weight handling, initialization, step size, and the precise use of weights during FKD need specification.

Appendix B provides valid standard discrepancy bounds under its assumptions, but limited explanation of the observed advantage. It neither compares the relevant constants nor connects the implemented feature-space squared-Wasserstein and image-recovery objectives to downstream risk. Its scalability criticism of characteristic-kernel MMD also overlooks minibatch estimators and the real-real kernel term being constant during synthetic-image optimization.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the scalability claims. Table 3 compares methods only on ImageNette at one image per class, where the target reduces to a mean. Table 5 adds Tiny ImageNet timings, but comparable ImageNet-1K measurements and clear accounting of teacher training, feature extraction, barycenter computation, and FKD are missing.
